topics.title: Performance vs scalability

kcs.statement: A system has a performance problem if it is slow for a single user, and a scalability problem if it is fast for one user but slows down under heavy load.
A service is scalable if adding resources increases its capacity (throughput) roughly in proportion to the resources added.

problem_ideas: A product page takes 4 s for a single test user: label it a performance or a scalability problem and name the first thing to profile
p99 latency is 80 ms at 1,000 QPS and 2 s at 5,000 QPS on the same code: classify the problem and say what the graph shows
Doubling servers from 4 to 8 raises throughput from 4,000 to 5,000 QPS: is the system scalable, and where might the shared bottleneck be?
Pick which of five incident reports describe scalability failures and which describe performance failures
An interviewer says 'make it scale': rewrite this as two measurable targets, one for latency and one for throughput
A batch job finishes in 10 min on 1 node and 9 min on 4 nodes: explain what likely limits it

lens.reason: Interviewers expect you to tell 'slow' apart from 'does not scale' before you propose fixes.

topics.title: Vertical vs horizontal scaling

kcs.statement: Vertical scaling adds CPU, memory or disk to one machine; it needs no code changes but hits a hardware ceiling and leaves that one machine as a point of failure.
Horizontal scaling adds more machines that share the load; capacity grows by adding nodes, but the application must tolerate any request landing on any node.
Scaling up is often the sensible first step because state stays on one machine; scaling out becomes necessary when one machine's capacity at peak QPS, or its availability, is no longer enough.

serves.reason: The high-level diagram must justify why the web tier is a pool of machines rather than one bigger box.

problem_ideas: A database server is at 85% CPU on 16 cores and the largest instance has 128 cores: how much headroom does scaling up buy, and what does it not fix?
A startup at 300 QPS asks whether to shard on day one: argue for scaling up first

List three code changes needed before a single-server app can be scaled horizontally
Compare cost: one 64-core machine vs eight 8-core machines when traffic is 10x higher at noon than at midnight
Failure story: the one big server reboots for a kernel patch and the whole site is down for 20 minutes; which scaling choice caused this?

topics.title: Stateless services and where session state goes

kcs.statement: A stateless service keeps no per-user session data in local memory between requests, so any instance can serve any request and instances can be added or removed freely.

To make a stateful web tier stateless, move session state to a shared store (a cache or database) or into a signed client token; sticky sessions are a workaround that skews load and loses sessions when a node dies.

serves.reason: Placing a load balancer in front of the app tier is only correct if that tier is stateless.

requires.reason: Statelessness is defined as the property that lets a tier scale horizontally.

problem_ideas: Shopping carts are stored in server memory and users lose them after a deploy: redesign so carts survive

Spot the hidden state: local file uploads, in-process rate counters, in-memory caches; which ones break horizontal scaling?

topics.title: Load balancers: what they do and why you need two

kcs.statement: A load balancer receives client traffic and spreads it across a pool of backend servers, taking servers out of rotation when periodic health probes fail.
Load balancers commonly terminate TLS, decrypting HTTPS once at the edge so backend servers handle plain HTTP inside the private network.
A single load balancer is itself a single point of failure, so production setups run at least two (active-passive or active-active) behind a shared virtual IP or multiple DNS records.

serves.reason: The diagram must place load balancers in front of each scaled-out tier.

requires.reason: A load balancer is defined as the component that distributes traffic across a horizontally scaled pool.

problem_ideas: Draw where the load balancers go for a three-tier app with web, API and database tiers

topics.title: Load balancing algorithms

kcs.statement: Round robin sends requests to servers in a fixed rotation; weighted round robin gives a server with weight w a share w/Σweights of requests, useful when servers differ in capacity.
Least-connections routes each new request to the server with the fewest active connections, which balances better than round robin when request durations vary widely.
IP-hash or key-hash routing sends the same client or key to the same server, giving affinity, but with hash-mod-N most keys move to a different server when N changes.

serves.reason: The outcome asks for a load-balancing choice justified against the workload.

requires.reason: Algorithms are the policy a load balancer uses to pick a backend.

problem_ideas: Implement weighted round robin for weights {A:3, B:1, C:1} and print the first 10 picks
Implement least-connections over a stream of (start, end) request events and report each server's peak load

topics.title: Layer 4 vs layer 7 load balancing

kcs.statement: A layer 4 load balancer routes on IP address and TCP/UDP port without reading the request content, so it is fast and protocol-agnostic but cannot route by URL path or header.
A layer 7 load balancer parses the HTTP request, so it can route by path, host or header (e.g. /api to one pool, /images to another) at the cost of more CPU and terminating the client connection.

serves.reason: Choosing L4 or L7 is part of justifying the load-balancing choice in the diagram.

requires.reason: Compares two kinds of load balancer.

problem_ideas: Route /video/* to a streaming pool and /api/* to the API pool: which layer is needed?

topics.title: Forward and reverse proxies

kcs.statement: A forward proxy acts on behalf of clients and hides them from servers; a reverse proxy sits in front of servers and hides them from clients.

A reverse proxy is useful even with one backend (TLS termination, compression, serving static files, hiding internal addresses), whereas a load balancer only adds value when there are several backends.

requires.reason: The key KC contrasts a reverse proxy with a load balancer.

topics.title: Content delivery networks

kcs.statement: A CDN serves static content (images, video, scripts, stylesheets) from edge servers close to users, cutting round trip time and offloading bandwidth from origin servers.
Users reach a nearby CDN edge through DNS-based routing or anycast, so asset URLs point at a CDN hostname rather than at the origin server.
Origin egress ≈ total egress × (1 − CDN hit ratio): at a 95% hit ratio, a 10 Gbps egress workload sends only 0.5 Gbps from the origin.

serves.reason: The outcome's diagram must place a CDN and justify it.

problem_ideas: Users in Mumbai see 300 ms per image from a US origin: estimate the saving with an edge 20 ms away

topics.title: Push vs pull CDNs

kcs.statement: A pull CDN fetches an object from the origin on its first request and keeps it until it expires; it suits high-traffic sites with large content sets, at the cost of slow first requests.
A push CDN stores content only when the origin uploads it; it suits small or rarely changing content sets and gives control over what is stored, but the origin must push every update.

serves.reason: The diagram's CDN choice is justified by picking push or pull for the content.

requires.reason: Both KCs describe how a CDN edge gets content from the origin server.

problem_ideas: A streaming service releases a new season at midnight to 5 million viewers: push or pull, and why?

topics.title: API gateways

kcs.statement: An API gateway is a single entry point that routes each client request to the right backend service and centralises cross-cutting concerns such as authentication, rate limiting and request logging.
Gateway aggregation lets one client call fan out to several backend services and combine their responses, reducing round trips for clients on slow mobile networks.

A load balancer spreads requests across identical instances of one service, while an API gateway routes between different services and applies policy; they are often layered, with the gateway in front of per-service load balancers.

serves.reason: Full mock answers to multi-service prompts need a gateway as the client entry point and the home for auth and rate limits.

requires.reason: Gateway routing is layer 7 routing by path and header; the lesson builds on it.
A gateway is a specialised reverse proxy, and the contrast is part of the KC.

topics.title: Service discovery and registries

kcs.statement: Service discovery keeps a registry of the live network locations of service instances, updated when instances register on start and removed when they stop or fail health probes.
In client-side discovery the caller queries the registry and picks an instance itself; in server-side discovery the caller sends to a load balancer or gateway that queries the registry for it.

topics.title: Rate limiting: why and where

kcs.statement: Rate limiting caps how many requests a client (identified by user, API key or IP) may make per time window, protecting backends from abuse, accidental overload and runaway cost.
A rate-limited HTTP request is rejected with status 429 Too Many Requests, ideally with a Retry-After header, and the limiter usually runs in the API gateway or middleware before business logic.

topics.title: The token bucket algorithm

kcs.statement: A token bucket holds up to C tokens, refills at r tokens per second, and admits a request only if at least one token is available, removing one token per admitted request.
A full token bucket admits a burst of up to C requests at once, then sustains r requests per second; with C=10 and r=2/s, 10 requests pass instantly and then one every 0.5 s.

requires.reason: The algorithm implements the rate limiting policy defined there.

problem_ideas: Implement allow(now) for a token bucket that refills lazily from elapsed time

topics.title: Fixed window, sliding window and leaky bucket

kcs.statement: A fixed-window counter allows N requests per clock-aligned window; it is cheap but can let up to 2N requests through in a short span around a window boundary.

A sliding-window log stores every request timestamp and counts those in the last window, which is exact but uses memory proportional to the request rate; a sliding-window counter approximates it by weighting the previous window's count.

A leaky bucket queues requests and processes them at a constant rate, turning bursts into a steady outflow and dropping requests when the queue is full, unlike a token bucket, which lets bursts through.

requires.reason: The leaky bucket KC is stated as a contrast with the token bucket.

problem_ideas: Limit 100/min with a fixed window: 100 requests at 0:59 and 100 at 1:01; how many pass, and why is that a problem?

topics.title: Rate limiting across many servers

kcs.statement: When N gateway instances enforce one limit with local counters, a client can exceed the limit by up to N times; a shared counter store (e.g. an in-memory key-value store) keeps one global count.
Read-then-write counter updates race under concurrency, so two requests can both take the last slot; an atomic increment, or one script that checks and updates together, prevents this.

requires.reason: Extends the single-node limiter to many nodes.

problem_ideas: 10 gateway nodes each allow 100/min locally: what is the worst-case global rate for one user?

topics.title: Assembling the request path for millions of users

kcs.statement: A typical web app scales in steps, each taken only when a measured bottleneck demands it: single server, then a separate database, then a load balancer over several stateless app servers, then a CDN for static assets, then caching, read replicas and sharding.

On a scaled request path, the client resolves DNS, fetches static assets from the CDN, and sends API calls through a load balancer or API gateway, where rate limits apply, to stateless application servers.
Each tier is sized only for the traffic that reaches it: if 80% of 50,000 peak requests/s are static assets served at a 95% CDN hit ratio, the origin sees 10,000 API QPS plus 2,000 asset misses.

serves.reason: This is the outcome's product: a diagram that places the LB, CDN and gateway, justified by the traffic each tier receives.

requires.reason: The tier-load KC uses the CDN hit ratio.
The request path places load balancers in front of the app tier.
Scaling the app tier depends on statelessness.
